issues.issue: Excluding "labor charges or freight charges" from commission cannot be applied directly under section 8, which makes commissions "payable based on invoices to the customer" — invoices that include freight and any labor. A court would have to decide whether commission is computed on the invoice total or on a net product figure.

The credit for "all orders accepted by the Company from their territory" runs only "as long as this Agreement remains in force," while section 8 makes commissions payable 45 days after the month of shipment, so orders accepted before termination may ship or be invoiced afterwards. The two provisions must be reconciled to know whether post-termination commissions are owed.

"Credited with all orders accepted by the Company from their territory" does not say whether an order is "from" the territory because the customer is located there or because the purchase order issued from there. "Credited" is also not equated with any right to payment.

"Accounts listed for collection will be written off and commissions deducted" does not say who lists an account, on what criteria, or when a write-off occurs, and "net amount collected" is not defined against collection costs. The chargeback mechanism therefore turns on an undefined internal act of the Company.

The 3% initial rate is said to be "subject to change" only on 30 days' notice by Registered Mail, which cannot be squared with section 11's automatic change to 5% on completion of the initial six months or with section 14's reserved right to set special rates. A court would have to decide whether the notice condition governs those changes.

The rate is stated by reference to an attached "Windfall Commission Policy" that is not part of the executed document, so a term the provision itself makes controlling is missing. The exception for "those customers as defined in Addendum A" also imports a roster the Company may redefine.

"New business" is nowhere defined and is "determined solely by Lovejoy Management," so the condition for the 8% rate rests entirely on one party's unreviewable characterization. The reporting duty to "John Est" (a garbled name) is also stated as a validation precondition without saying what happens if it is not met.

The 8% new-business rate overlaps with section 9, which sets 3% on all "shipments to customers in the Representative's territory" during the same initial six months, and neither provision subordinates itself to the other. A court would have to decide which rate applies to a shipment that is both.

"The payable commission rate for all business" at 5% cannot be read literally alongside the no-commission categories in section 7(a)-(d) and the reduced rates permitted by section 12 and the special rates reserved by section 14. A court would have to decide how far "all business" is cut back by those provisions.

The reduced-rate accounts exist only in "Addendum B (if applicable to the Representative)," and no Addendum B accompanies the agreement, so the provision identifies no accounts and no rates. Whether any reduction was ever agreed is left to be proved outside the document.

Paying commission to the Representative "in whose territory the Purchase Order originates" uses a different test from section 7, which credits the Representative with "all orders accepted by the Company from their territory," and from section 9, which measures commission by "shipments to customers in the Representative's territory." A court would have to decide which locus controls a split-territory sale.

The reserved right to set "special commission rates" whenever the "competitive situation, in the Company's judgment," warrants it cannot be squared with the fixed 5% of section 11 or with section 9's requirement of 30 days' Registered Mail notice before any rate change. A court would have to decide whether section 14 overrides those rate provisions.

The duty to "assist in the collection of past due accounts" sets no standard, scope or cost allocation for the assistance required, and "unrated new accounts" and "full information" are equally open. A court would have to supply content to measure any breach.

Termination for cause requires the "other party's unreasonable and repeated failure to perform," a standard that is undefined and doubly qualified, and the notice sentence is grammatically broken ("mailed via certified or registered to") so the sequence of notice, cure and termination is uncertain. A court would have to construe what conduct and what notice suffice.

The termination provision says nothing about commissions on orders accepted or shipped after termination, which must be read against section 7's limit of credit to "as long as this Agreement remains in force" and section 8's payment 45 days after the month of shipment. The parties' post-termination positions emerge only from reading the three together.
